extra.message: Server-Side Template Injection in 404 handler — attacker crafts a URL like /{{7*7}} or a Jinja RCE gadget path to achieve remote code execution via SSTI [verified: request.path is attacker-controlled and interpolated directly into an f-string then passed to render_template_string with no escaping, enabling SSTI/RCE.]

Server-Side Template Injection via request.path in 404 handler — Full remote code execution on the server by requesting a URL such as `/{{ self.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}` or a Jinja RCE gadget chain, since attacker input is compiled and executed as a Jinja template. [verified: Same as idx 0: request.path flows unescaped into render_template_string via f-string, confirmed SSTI/RCE with no intervening control.]

Mass assignment of is_admin via account update form — Any authenticated non-admin user can self-promote to admin by including is_admin=true in the POST /account body, gaining full admin privileges (e.g. access to /registration-codes management). [verified: update_account() (routes/account.py) has no @login_required or admin check even, and merges all non-None AccountForm fields including is_admin (BooleanField in forms/account_form.py:8) directly into current_user.__dict__ then commits, letting any authenticated (or given the missing login_required, potentially any) user self-promote to admin.]

SQL injection in note search — attacker can inject arbitrary SQL to read/modify other users' notes or exfiltrate data from the SQLite DB [verified: search_param is f-string spliced into text() with no parameterization, reachable by any logged-in user via /search?search=.]

Missing auth + mass assignment allows privilege escalation to admin — an unauthenticated request (or any user) can set is_admin=true on their account, escalating to admin privileges and gaining access to registration-codes management [verified: AccountForm includes is_admin and update_account mass-assigns all non-None form fields (except password) onto current_user.__dict__ with no field filtering, allowing privilege escalation; route also lacks @login_required.]

Insecure deserialization of client-controlled cookie — attacker crafts a malicious pickle payload in the 'preferences' cookie to achieve remote code execution on the server [verified: before_request unconditionally pickle.loads(b64decode()) on the fully client-controlled 'preferences' cookie with no signature check, giving RCE via crafted pickle.]

SQL injection in registration code validation — attacker can bypass registration-code gating or run arbitrary SQL against the DB to enumerate/alter codes and other tables [verified: code comes only from wtforms Length(min=5) validation with no character restriction and is interpolated raw via f-string into text(), so attacker input reaches the SQL sink unsanitized (routes/signup.py:17).]

Hardcoded Flask secret key — attacker who knows/guesses the secret key can forge session cookies to impersonate any user, including admins [verified: app.secret_key is a static hardcoded string signing session cookies, allowing forged/tampered sessions for anyone who obtains this public value.]

Hardcoded default credentials and static registration code — If deployed without changing these seeds, an attacker can log in as the default admin account (admin@evfa.com/admin) or use the static registration code to self-register, bypassing the intended signup gate. [verified: db_seed.py:16-19 always seeds admin@evfa.com/admin with is_admin=True on first run; if deployed without changing seed data, this is a trivial full-admin credential compromise, more severe than the registration-code bypass alone.]

IDOR on personal notes endpoint — Any authenticated user can enumerate other users' private notes by changing the `user_id` path parameter. [verified: Duplicate of finding 2/7: confirmed IDOR, only @login_required gate, no ownership check on user_id.]

Missing authentication decorator on account update route — Inconsistent enforcement of authentication increases risk that unauthenticated requests reach account-mutating logic; combined with the mass-assignment bug this compounds the privilege-escalation risk. [verified: Duplicate of finding 6: update_account missing @login_required decorator confirmed by direct code read.]

Unauthenticated state-changing endpoint reusing insecure pickle cookie — Unauthenticated/cross-site requests can manipulate and perpetuate the insecure pickled preferences cookie, compounding the deserialization attack surface [verified: toggle_darkmode lacks @login_required and any CSRF protection, and the pickled preferences cookie is deserialized unconditionally in before_request regardless of route, so unauthenticated/cross-site requests can trigger and perpetuate pickle deserialization cycles.]

IDOR on note deletion — Any authenticated user can delete arbitrary other users' notes, causing data loss/tampering across accounts [verified: Confirmed identical to finding 0 — no ownership check exists between session.get(Note, note_id) and session.delete(note).]

Missing CSRF protection on registration-code creation — A malicious page can force an authenticated admin's browser to mint new registration codes, bypassing the signup gate [verified: No CSRFProtect/WTF_CSRF found repo-wide, and add_registration_codes only checks current_user.is_admin with no CSRF token, so an authenticated admin's browser can be forced via CSRF to mint new registration codes.]

SSRF via profile image URL fetch — attacker can make the server issue arbitrary requests to internal services or cloud metadata endpoints, potentially exfiltrating credentials or pivoting into internal network [verified: urlopen(url) is called with fully user-controlled url from ImageForm with no scheme/host allow-list, enabling SSRF to internal/metadata endpoints or file:// reads.]

Hardcoded static registration/signup bypass code — Attacker who has seen the source (public repo) can self-register on any fresh deployment using the known static code, bypassing the intended invite-only signup control [verified: db_seed.py:9 hardcodes a static registration code that is always inserted on first run and is public in source; anyone can use it at /signup to bypass the invite gate on any unconfigured deployment.]

Missing CSRF protection on state-changing endpoints — attacker can craft a malicious page that submits forms on behalf of an authenticated victim to change account/password/is_admin, delete notes, or add registration codes [verified: No CSRF token generation/validation anywhere in app.py or routes; all POST routes are exploitable via cross-site form submission.]

Missing CSRF protection on state-changing account routes — Attacker-controlled site can force a logged-in victim's browser to submit account changes (including is_admin escalation) or password changes without consent. [verified: Same missing CSRF protection confirmed across /account, /account/image, /notes routes; duplicate of finding 4 but independently valid.]

Sensitive data exposure via SQLAlchemy query logging — Credentials, registration codes, and other sensitive query parameters are written to application logs, increasing exposure if logs are aggregated, stored, or leaked. [verified: models/__init__.py:14 sets echo=True unconditionally on the engine with no environment/debug guard, so every SQL statement and its bound parameters (e.g., plaintext passwords prior to hashing, registration codes) is logged to stdout in normal operation.]

Account enumeration via distinct signup error messages — Attacker can determine which email addresses are already registered, aiding credential-stuffing and targeted phishing/reset attacks [verified: do_signup checks user existence before returning distinct 'User already exists' vs 'Invalid registration code' messages (signup.py:47-59), but this branch is only reached if the attacker already supplies a valid registration code, limiting real-world exploitability to insiders/leaked codes.]

Unbounded response buffering and no timeout in profile image fetch — Attacker-controlled URL fetch can exhaust server memory (unbounded read) or hang worker threads indefinitely (no timeout), causing denial of service. [verified: Same missing timeout/size-limit issue as [1]; duplicate finding of the unbounded read/no-timeout condition, confirmed but low severity DoS.]
